title: Dean
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood recalls Dean, a first grader he tutored in a small Napa reading clinic more than forty years ago. Dean could comprehend third-grade stories when read aloud but treated print as a string of words to be called out, not as speech written down. Underwood's response was to put meaning first through the Language Experience Approach and word analysis second, with explicit phonics work alongside. Looking back, he lists what he did not yet know, including metacognition, think-alouds and collaboration with the classroom teacher. The case becomes an argument for reading specialists trained in a professional knowledge base.
points: Dean's case shows a child with strong oral language and listening comprehension who still failed to expect print to make sense.
Underwood's approach was meaning first, word analysis second, pairing read-alouds and discussion with systematic decoding practice.
Reflecting years later, he identifies missed levers such as modelling thinking, think-alouds and sharing assessment information with the classroom teacher.
The story argues that children like Dean need reading specialists with a real professional knowledge base.
quotes: But he did not expect print to make sense. His first year of school had taught him that reading was one word at a time, seeing a word, recognizing it or not, moving on to the next word.
My objective in working with him was first to instill in him the expectation that print would have meaning just as speech has meaning. I would put making sense first, word analysis second.

To that end, when we worked on connected text at his instructional level, I read the passage aloud to him first as he followed along with his eyes, we talked about the overall meaning, and then we sounded out or broke apart single words used in the passage.
Dean also needed work in decoding isolated words of the type described in Words Their Way4 to build his capacity to use phonics as a tool to unlock unfamiliar words.

But I had not yet learned about metacognition, the central executive function, the zone of proximal development. I knew nothing of the think aloud as a research, assessment, or instructional technique.
It did not occur to me to collaborate with his classroom teacher. I could have incorporated stories she read aloud in class into my interactions with him.
He signifies for me the need for reading specialists trained in a professional knowledge base. Not all children need such a specialist, but those who do face a difficult road without attention.
